en: The Ritual Manual for the Flying Alms Bowl of the Mantra-Holding Rishi,
composed by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery, the Great Ācārya:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to purify their preparatory practices and [attain] the power of flight..."

Regarding the use of an alms-bowl to perform Buddha-work: first, select a deep mountain or secluded valley where *bìluó* vines and soft, lush grasses cover the ground, a place where strange birds and wondrous beasts gather, where *xiānren* (immortals) soar and sages and *ūdāras* dwell in profound seclusion—a place utterly remote from human contact and shunned by the worldly.
One should then take one *dǒu* of non-glutinous rice and carry it for a hundred days.

Abiding on a high mountain peak like a cloud-formation, with a physical form resembling an overturned bowl or an upturned bowl, in the depths of a secluded cave where no one dwells, first observe the fast and precepts for forty-nine days; next, fast for one day;
next, fast for three days; then eat one *droṇa* of rice per day until the non-glutinous rice is exhausted, maintaining complete purity throughout.
The Dharma-holding Vajra-ācārya should recite the mantras of the Eight Great Nāga Kings according to his capacity;
he must not be negligent, day and night invoking the names of the Great Nāga Kings, namely:
Nanda Nāgarāja, Upananda Nāgarāja, Sāgara Nāgarāja, Vāsuki Nāgarāja, Takṣaka Nāgarāja, and Ananta [Nāgarāja].
The Nāga King Vāsuki is one of the eight great Nāga Kings and is the mount of the *ṛṣis* who maintain these mantras.
He follows all ascetic śramaṇas and obeys their every command; by means of his bowl, he can cause the trichiliocosm to revolve simultaneously at will.
Following the practitioner's thought, he can reach the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the eighteen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
They travel in a mere instant to the four formless realms, even to other infinite worlds,
and reach the presence of Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the kings of great wheel-turning monarchs, minor wheel-turning monarchs, the sixteen kings,
the five thousand petty kings, and the various scattered rulers, as well as their palaces, queens, consorts, and princes.

Whether it be the families of princesses, great ministers, or the various officials who manifest the desires of those practicing, or who travel to and fro displaying great supernormal powers to subdue sentient beings of false views—such sovereign mastery is entirely due to the power of the Dragon King.
Therefore, you must protect and uphold this with a single-minded focus; do not allow your minds to be distracted. I shall now speak its truth.
It is said:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ nantu upanantu ye svāhā*.
When one has recited this mantra three hundred thousand times, the Dragon King of the Great Ocean and the Dragon King Anavatapta [will appear].
All the great dragon kings, all the great dragon kings, will manifest in human form and assemble at the place where the practitioner performs their ascetic practices.
With palms joined and prostrating upon the ground, they will take refuge and pay homage. At that time, one should cover the ground with the alms bowl and recite the mantra over it seven times;
the dragon kings will then support it and carry it through the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, throughout the heavens above and the earth below.
The Asuras brought mountain yams from their palace; when the practitioner consumes them, his life span reaches a thousand years.
From that time forward, he will manifest great supernormal transformations at will, possessing sovereign spiritual powers and majestic virtue all at once.
All devas, nāga kings, māra kings, and human kings will come to take refuge in him. If, when reciting over the alms bowl, it does not fly up quickly, one should recite the mantra to urge it on.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām (1) oṃ nantu upanantu ye (2) kinnarāye (3) paripūraya (4) kiṅkarāṇāṃ svāhā (5).
*Tad yathā svāhā.* Reciting this mantra,
the Dragon King Dahrila shall arouse great valor and speedily fly with his powerful head-bowl to the worlds of the ten directions in a single thought-moment,
transforming beings according to their conditions. I shall now recite the Dragon King’s Seal-Mantra (*mudrā-vidyā*).
The practitioner should place the left and right palms together, alternating their positions, for the rite will be swiftly accomplished; do not harbor doubts.
This secret method was constantly maintained by the Great Sages of old and manifests great supernatural power.
If anyone practices this method on the first, eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the bright fortnight in the first, fifth, or ninth month, [the result will be attained].

On the twenty-third, twenty-ninth, or thirtieth day of the dark fortnight, having bathed cleanly and put on fresh, pure garments, one should sit upon white *kuśa* grass, maintaining firm vows of fasting.
One must abstain from all five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*), impure fish, meat, and the like;
avoid the company of women; and distance oneself from all worldly distractions and afflictions until reaching a state of utter purity where no other person is present.
Dwell in a thatched hut and take delight in solitude and tranquility; subsist only on grass leaves, wood fruits, stones, and grits.
Day and night recite mantras; before three years have passed, you shall achieve the "empty bowl" (the state of non-attachment).

Do not recite other mantras, do not engage in worldly entanglements, but maintain a single-minded focus on reciting this one mantra alone. Do not concern yourself with what cannot be discerned, and do not be stingy or greedy regarding the blessings and rewards you obtain.
Universally bestowing upon sentient beings and extensively performing Buddha-works—if one acts with a greedy mind, the bowl will not extend and will not fly;
those who are able to be cautious must not be indolent.
*The Ritual for Flying the Bowl*.
On the seventh day of the first month of the second year of Kenkū, the *Sōjō* (Archbishop) of Daijō-in at Mufūji received the transmission of this text from beginning to end.
In the spring of the third month of the fifth year of Bunka, the year of Ren-ge (1842), [it was transcribed] using a manuscript preserved at Shinnyo-in on Tōeizan.
Copied and proofread once from the first watch of the day; by Longgan.
